query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating corrosion‐inhibiting refractory elements like chromium and hafnium into a high‐entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of a stable, self-healing protective oxide layer (e.g., Cr2O3 and HfO2) when exposed to molten aluminum at around 660°C, thereby significantly reducing corrosion and erosion of the dipping and plating equipment parts.
generation.material_initial_state: Prepare parts currently made from conventional engineering metals (e.g., standard steels or nickel‐based superalloys) that are rapidly corroded by high-temperature liquid aluminum.
generation.intervention: Develop and use a specially designed refractory high‐entropy alloy that includes refractory and corrosion‐inhibiting elements (notably Cr and Hf) via methods such as powder metallurgy or spark plasma sintering.
generation.conditions: Long-term exposure to molten aluminum at approximately 660°C, as experienced during the hot-dip aluminum plating process.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dense, adherent, and self-healing oxide scale (primarily Cr2O3 and HfO2) on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: At 660°C, the alloy’s tailored composition preferentially oxidizes to form a compact oxide layer that acts as a diffusion barrier, preventing aggressive molten aluminum from corroding the underlying material.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy should exhibit a significantly lower corrosion rate and extend the service life of the dipping and plating equipment parts compared to conventional materials.
generation.baseline: The rapid deterioration and short service life observed in current equipment parts made from conventional metals due to corrosion by molten aluminum.
generation.boundary: While the hypothesis is formulated for the specific operational conditions encountered in hot-dip aluminum plating (~660°C), the long-term stability of the protective oxide layer under cyclic thermal stresses and potential contaminants remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantification of life-extension and corrosion rate reduction is uncertain, and further testing is needed to validate the durability of the protective oxide scale under practical operating conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate samples of the proposed refractory high-entropy alloy with added Cr and Hf and comparative samples of conventional metals. Expose both sets to molten aluminum at 660°C over prolonged periods under controlled laboratory conditions. Periodically assess the formation and integrity of oxide scales and measure the corrosion rates.
measurements: Surface and cross-sectional analysis using SEM/EDS
X-ray diffraction (XRD) to identify oxide phases
Microstructural evaluation of oxide scale adhesion and uniformity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy does not form a stable, protective oxide layer or if its corrosion rate under molten aluminum exposure is not significantly lower than that of conventional materials, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

decision.trend: Earlier research in refractory high‐entropy alloys has focused on achieving high‐temperature stability and oxidation resistance by tailoring alloy compositions and microstructures. For example, one study (PMC7513042) used advanced powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering to introduce in situ ceramic reinforcements, thereby enhancing both mechanical strength and oxidation resistance at high temperatures. Later work (PMC10154406) further demonstrated that designing quinary refractory alloys could yield excellent thermal stability and resistance under extreme conditions. In both cases, the focus was on modifying the material composition to improve its performance in aggressive, high‐temperature environments, even though the specific challenge of corrosion by molten aluminum was not directly addressed.
decision.unsolved: What remains unsolved is the development of a material that not only withstands high temperatures, but also exhibits long‐term chemical inertness against direct contact with highly aggressive, molten aluminum. In particular, strategies for tailoring alloy compositions to form self‐protective oxide layers that resist aluminum erosion during the plating process have not yet been explored.
decision.lever: introduction of refractory and corrosion‐inhibiting elements
decision.why: Following the trend in refractory HEA development—where compositional tuning has led to alloys capable of withstanding high-temperature oxidation and extreme conditions—the most plausible next step is to design an alloy specifically for molten aluminum environments. By incorporating elements such as chromium and hafnium (or similar corrosion‐inhibiting refractory elements) that can promote the formation of a stable, protective oxide film, researchers can directly target the challenge of long-term aluminum erosion. This approach occupies the open‐question niche using material composition changes as the primary lever, aligning with the cues of the research question.
